title: Why Every Big Expense Costs More Than Planned
hook_text: WHY BIG EXPENSES ALWAYS COST MORE

beats.say: The repair always costs more than the plan. That's a known bias, not bad luck.
beats.visual: Extreme close-up of a broken car transmission resting on wet rain-slick asphalt beneath a single cold sodium street light.

beats.say: You carefully budget $3,000 for a home repair, a move, or a holiday.
beats.visual: Silhouette of a person standing inside a gutted room at blue hour, extreme high angle shot.

beats.say: But when final bills arrive, you end up paying $4,500 out of pocket instead.
beats.visual: Low angle shot of paper invoices fluttering across a wet dark concrete underpass at night.

beats.say: Why does almost every major expense quietly blow past your original budget?
beats.visual: Wide shot of a massive unfinished concrete bridge tower shrouded in thick morning fog.

beats.say: Most people assume unexpected surprises hit them out of nowhere just this once.
beats.visual: Extreme high angle of a lone figure walking across a vast empty industrial parking lot in cold fluorescent light.

beats.say: Psychologists call this common cognitive trap the Planning Fallacy.
beats.visual: Extreme close-up of dark architectural plans resting on rusted metal lit by a single beam of practical light.

beats.say: Your brain naturally plans for the absolute best-case scenario while ignoring past overruns.
beats.visual: Low angle silhouette of a person looking up at a towering glass skyscraper under orange sodium streetlights.

beats.say: Even after your last project went over budget, you still expect the next one to run smoothly.
beats.visual: Rain-slick street at night reflecting flickering neon light beside heavy stacked moving boxes.

beats.say: Here's the counter-move to protect your bank account from your own optimism.
beats.visual: Top-down extreme wide view of an empty wet highway cutting through a dark forest at dusk.

beats.say: Step one: never build a budget based on ideal quotes or best-case timelines.
beats.visual: Macro shot of a heavy iron padlock on a wet dark wooden surface under cold blue hour light.

beats.say: Step two: look at what the last similar project actually cost, and add 30%.
beats.visual: Silhouette of a hand marking a dark leather notebook beside a solitary desk lamp on an empty tower floor.

beats.say: When you anchor your budget to historical reality instead of hope, your money stays intact.
beats.visual: Cinematic wide shot of a quiet open water harbor at blue hour with distant sodium skyline lights.

beats.say: Stop letting bad plans drain your paycheck. Follow for the money rules school never taught you.
beats.visual: Low angle silhouette of a person standing on a wet city ridge line overlooking foggy city lights.

caption: Why do your projects always go over budget? It's not bad luck—it's the Planning Fallacy. #money #personalfinance #moneypsychology #wealth #mindset
description: Learn why big expenses routinely cost more than your initial estimates. Discover the psychological bias known as the Planning Fallacy and the simple counter-move to protect your savings.
first_comment: What was the last project or expense that went way over your original budget?

facts.claim: People underestimate the time and cost of tasks even when aware that past tasks took longer and cost more.
facts.basis: Planning Fallacy, documented psychological bias identified by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky (1979).

loop_map.stakes: Budgeting $3,000 for a plan only to get hit with a $4,500 bill.
loop_map.big_question: Why does almost every major expense quietly blow past your original budget?
loop_map.assume: Surprises and bad luck hit out of nowhere just this once.
loop_map.reveal: The Planning Fallacy makes your brain ignore past overruns and plan exclusively for best-case scenarios.
